content: 1. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported in patients treated with nucleoside analogs, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals, including emtricitabine. These cases have predominantly occurred in women. Risk factors may include obesity and prolonged exposure to nucleoside analogs. 2. Extreme caution should be exercised when administering nucleoside analogs to patients with known risk factors for liver disease. However, cases of lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis have also been reported in patients without any known risk factors. 3. Treatment with emtricitabine should be discontinued in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity. This includes findings such as hepatomegaly and steatosis, even in the absence of marked elevations in transaminase levels. 4. All patients with HIV-1 should be tested for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection before initiating antiretroviral therapy. Emtricitabine is not approved for the treatment of chronic HBV infection, and its safety and efficacy in patients co-infected with HBV and HIV-1 have not been established. 5. Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who discontinue emtricitabine. In some cases, these exacerbations have been associated with liver decompensation and liver failure in patients infected with HBV and treated with emtricitabine. 6. Patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV who discontinue emtricitabine should have hepatic function closely monitored with clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least several months. If appropriate, initiation of anti-HBV therapy may be warranted. 7. Emtricitabine is a component of several fixed-dose combination products, including Atripla, Complera, Stribild, and Truvada. It should not be co-administered with these products. 8. Due to similarities between emtricitabine and lamivudine, emtricitabine should not be co-administered with other drugs containing lamivudine, such as Combivir, Epivir, Epivir-HBV, Epzicom, or Trizivir. 9. Emtricitabine is primarily eliminated by the kidneys. Dosage adjustments are recommended for patients with impaired renal function to prevent drug accumulation and potential toxicity. 10. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. This may include central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these changes are not fully understood, and a causal relationship has not been established. 11. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including emtricitabine. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with recovering immune systems may develop an inflammatory response to indolent or residual opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium infection, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), or tuberculosis. These conditions may require further evaluation and treatment. 12. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves' disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution. However, the onset of these conditions is more variable and can occur many months after the initiation of antiretroviral therapy.
